scenes.heading: Client Libraries — Advanced Features (Part 2 of 2)
scenes.narration: Templates. Client Libraries — Advanced Features (Part 2 of 2). In this video we review 6 key concepts you need to know for the certification.

scenes.question: How do you expose an /apps-restricted client library to visitors while keeping /apps access-restricted?
scenes.heading: Creating a client library folder under /etc that embeds the library located under /apps
scenes.body: To keep /apps restricted from website visitors while still delivering its client library code, you create a client library folder under /etc that embeds the /apps client library, using the embed property with the value of the target's categories property.

scenes.question: How does embedding help minimize requests on a page with many client libraries?
scenes.heading: It combines all necessary client library code into a single file, reducing the number of <script> requests during page load
scenes.body: Embedding lets you combine all necessary client library code into a single file via the embed property, consolidating multiple libraries and reducing the number of separate requests made during page load.

scenes.question: When CSS is embedded from one client library into another, how are relative resource paths (like background images) resolved?
scenes.heading: Relative to the embedding library's location, not the original embedded library's location
scenes.body: When you embed CSS files from one client library into another, the generated CSS code contains paths relative to the embedding library's location, not the original library's — so a rule like background: url(images/bg.jpg) resolves relative to where the embedding library lives.

scenes.question: How do you inspect exactly which files are being embedded at runtime in a client library?
scenes.heading: Append ?debugClientLibs=true to the URL — it shows @import statements instead of the merged, embedded code
scenes.body: Enable debug mode by appending ?debugClientLibs=true to the page URL. This displays the names of embedded files as @import statements in the generated library, instead of the actual embedded code, letting you verify dependencies.

scenes.question: What are AEM's built-in CSS/JS preprocessors, and which is the default?
scenes.heading: YUI Compressor is the default; Google Closure Compiler (GCC) for JavaScript is available as a pluggable alternative
scenes.body: AEM ships with built-in support for YUI Compressor (CSS and JavaScript) and Google Closure Compiler (JavaScript), with YUI set as the default preprocessor. Preprocessors can be configured per-library or system-wide.

scenes.question: What tool lets you discover all client library folders and preview the generated output for a category?
scenes.heading: The /libs/cq/granite/components/dumplibs/dumplibs component, via the dumplibs.html/.test.html URLs
scenes.body: The /libs/cq/granite/components/dumplibs/dumplibs component generates a page listing all client library folders, their categories and dependencies, accessible at dumplibs.html (with a Test Output page for previewing generated code per category).
